opus-5.5.text:
I think the answer is: both, and the balance depends on who the environment was built for.

If you look at it from first principles, code and APIs are the most natural interface for a model. They're text, they're compositional, they're precise, and the feedback is very clear: the program runs or it doesn't, the API returns something or an error. A lot of the most powerful agents today are really coding agents, because code gives you a huge, expressive action space that's still machine-friendly. So wherever an API exists, or wherever you can write code to get something done, an agent should usually prefer that. It's faster, cheaper, and more reliable than clicking around.

But the reality is that most of the digital world was built for humans, not machines. There's a long tail of websites, enterprise software, and legacy systems that will never have a clean API, because nobody had the incentive to build one. If you want an agent to be generally useful, to do the things a person can do on a computer, it has to be able to use the graphical interface too. In that sense GUI ability is a kind of universal fallback. It's the interface that's guaranteed to exist.

So I see it a bit like how humans work. A good engineer writes a script when the task is repetitive and there's a programmatic path, and uses the UI when that's the easiest way in. Agents will develop a similar judgment about which interface to use.

Longer term, I think the environment will co-evolve with the agents. Once agents become a major class of users, people will start building products for them: more APIs, more machine-readable interfaces, maybe new protocols designed specifically for agents. Historically, interfaces adapt to their users. We built GUIs because humans became computer users; we'll build agent-native interfaces as agents become users. The GUI won't disappear, because humans still need it, but the share of work that goes through code and APIs will probably grow a lot.

And one more point: the hard part isn't really the interface itself. Whether it's clicking or calling an API, the deeper challenge is reasoning, long-horizon planning, and knowing what the user actually wants. The interface is the hands; the real question is the brain and the context.

r001.rationale: The response discusses code and APIs as related but distinct options; it never states that APIs are a subset of code-based interfaces.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says agents will use “both” and describes using APIs or code where available and graphical interfaces for human-built systems.

r003.rationale: It says many existing systems will lack APIs and that GUI ability is needed, but does not judge that enabling GUI use is easier than converting those interfaces into APIs.

fable-5.1.text:
I think in the long run it's going to be mostly code and APIs, with GUIs as a fallback rather than the main channel.

The reason is pretty simple. A graphical interface is a compression layer designed for human perception. It takes structured state and renders it into pixels, buttons, menus, because that's what we're good at parsing. For an agent, that's a detour. You take something that was already structured, flatten it into an image, and then ask the model to reconstruct the structure by looking at a screenshot. It works, and the computer-use demos are impressive, but it's inherently lossy and slow. Code and APIs are the native language of the machine. They're precise, they're composable, you can verify them, and you can chain them without a human in the loop.

So why do we still care about GUIs at all? Because the world wasn't built for agents. There's a huge long tail of software, websites, internal tools, legacy systems that have no API, or where the API is incomplete. If you want an agent to be useful today, in the environment that actually exists, it has to be able to operate the interface humans use. That's the pragmatic reason computer-use agents matter right now. It's a bridge.

But I think the interesting dynamic is that the environment will adapt. When a large share of your "users" are agents, you start exposing things differently. We already see this with things like MCP, with companies shipping agent-facing endpoints, with documentation being written for models rather than for people. The economic pressure goes in one direction: if your service is easier for agents to call programmatically, agents will use it more, and you win. So I'd expect the GUI-only surface area to shrink over time, not because GUIs disappear for humans, but because almost everything will grow a machine-facing layer alongside the human-facing one.

The other thing I'd say is that code is more than just an interface, it's a reasoning medium. When an agent writes a script to accomplish something, it's externalizing a plan into something that's checkable and reusable. That's very different from clicking through a sequence of buttons, where the "plan" lives only in the trajectory. That's part of why I've always felt that language models acting through code is such a natural fit. The action space is open-ended, it's expressive, and the feedback is sharp.

So my picture is: in the near term, a hybrid, with vision-based GUI control filling the gaps. In the long term, agents primarily talking to the world through code and APIs, and the GUI becoming something agents use mostly when they need to do what a human would do, or when they're working alongside a human and need to share the same view.

r001.rationale: The response discusses code and APIs together but does not state that APIs are a subset of code-based interfaces.

r002.rationale: It predicts a hybrid near term and says agents will primarily use code and APIs long term while still using GUIs when needed or alongside humans.

r003.rationale: It says agents need to operate existing interfaces because many lack APIs, but does not judge that this is easier than converting those interfaces into APIs.

astra-6.text:
I think in the long run, agents will probably use code and APIs for a lot of things, because those interfaces are more direct. If you want to retrieve some information or execute an operation, you don’t necessarily want to render a webpage, take a screenshot, and figure out where to click. With an API, the inputs and outputs are more explicit, and it’s easier to check whether the operation succeeded.

But there’s a difference between that long-term direction and what’s useful today. A lot of software only exposes its full functionality through a graphical interface. And companies aren’t going to redesign all their software before agents can use it. So being able to use the same interface as a human is a very powerful way for an agent to work with existing systems.

I also wouldn’t put code and graphical interfaces into completely separate categories. An agent might write code to process data, use an API to retrieve it, and then open a browser to inspect the result. The important capability is choosing the right interface for each step.

So my expectation is that graphical interfaces will provide broad access, while more of the frequent, well-defined operations will move toward APIs or other machine-friendly interfaces. Humans may still want to see a visual representation to understand and supervise what’s happening, even when the agent is doing the underlying work through code.

r001.rationale: The response discusses code and APIs alongside each other but never states that APIs are a subset of code-based interfaces.

r002.rationale: It predicts agents will use APIs for frequent operations and graphical interfaces for broad access, and describes combining code, APIs, and a browser.

r003.rationale: It says existing software often exposes full functionality only through a graphical interface and companies will not redesign it before agents can use it, presenting use of the human interface as a practical path for working with existing systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think agents will use both, but code and APIs will probably be the preferred interface wherever they’re available. If you can accomplish something with a function call, it’s usually faster, cheaper, and easier to verify than clicking through a graphical interface. You also get structured outputs, which makes it easier to compose multiple steps.

But graphical interfaces matter because the world isn’t fully exposed through APIs. A lot of software was built for humans, and an agent that can only call APIs is limited to what developers have explicitly made accessible. Being able to use a browser or a computer gives the agent a much broader space of possible actions.

So I don’t see this as choosing one interface forever. An agent might use an API to retrieve data, write code to analyze it, and then use a graphical interface to finish a task in an application. The important capability is selecting the right tool and switching between them. Over time, as more software is designed with agents in mind, I would expect more of that interaction to happen through code and structured interfaces.

r001.rationale: It discusses APIs and code as preferred interfaces but does not state that APIs are a subset of code-based interfaces.

r002.rationale: It predicts agents will use both, describing code/APIs alongside graphical interfaces and switching between them.

r003.rationale: It says graphical interfaces broaden access to software not exposed through APIs, but does not compare enabling agents to use those interfaces with converting them all into APIs.
